headline: Connecticut preservation council asks AG to halt Manchester home demolition
dek: The state panel is challenging the town’s plan to replace an 1886 Cheney mill-worker home with about 20 parking spaces beside Manchester’s new public library.
body: Connecticut’s Historic Preservation Council has unanimously asked the state attorney general to intervene before Manchester can demolish a historic two-family home for library parking, putting a local land-use dispute into a state-level preservation review. The council’s Oct. 7 agenda identified 29-31 Eldridge Street as a threatened property, and the vote reported by [CT Insider](https://www.ctinsider.com/journalinquirer/article/manchester-ct-eldridge-street-library-parking-22467008.php) asks the attorney general to consider stopping the proposed destruction under Connecticut’s environmental-protection law.

The immediate issue is a town-owned property next to Manchester’s new Main Street library. CT Insider reported that Manchester bought the Eldridge Street two-family home in June for $455,000 and plans to remove it to create roughly 20 additional parking spaces. The building sits within the Cheney Brothers Historic District and was built in 1886 as worker housing associated with the Cheney Brothers silk mills, according to testimony summarized in the report. The purchase was made for a public project, but the council’s action means the town’s preferred use of the parcel is now subject to a preservation challenge.

Manchester officials have argued that the parking is part of making the new library function for the public. Town Manager Steve Stephanou told CT Insider that the building has been poorly maintained and described it as an eyesore. He said the town’s library plans included 54 spaces and that the additional spaces could be used for employees, while removing the house would also improve a blind spot at the back of the lot. Those are the town’s stated operational and safety reasons; they do not establish that demolition will occur or that the attorney general will accept the council’s recommendation.

Opponents say the town has not shown that demolition is the only feasible way to meet its parking needs. Brad Schide of Preservation Connecticut argued that the structure should be rehabilitated and kept in its existing two-family configuration. Architect Dave Goslin told the council that the house needs work but rated its underlying quality highly, and he suggested that Manchester could sell it to a preservation-minded developer. He also described a possible compromise that would keep the house while removing the garage for about 10 spaces, although he warned that the resulting lot would be substandard.

The dispute matters beyond one building because the house is part of a larger historic landscape. CT Insider reported that the area was designated a National Historic Landmark in 1978. Preservation advocates told the council that removing one surviving worker house could weaken the character of the district and make future losses easier to justify. Manchester officials, by contrast, said they were not seeking a broader demolition program and viewed this parcel as a special case because it borders the library project and has been in poor condition.

The state panel’s role is more than an advisory review of architectural taste. The [Connecticut Department of Economic and Community Development](https://portal.ct.gov/decd/content/historic-preservation/06_about_shpo/historic-preservation-council) says the Historic Preservation Council is created by state law and is authorized to work with the Office of the Attorney General to prevent the unreasonable destruction of properties listed on, or being considered for listing on, the National Register of Historic Places. The council’s [official Oct. 7 agenda](https://portal.ct.gov/-/media/decd/historic-preservation/06_about_shpo/hpc-agendas/october-7-2026-hpc-meeting-agenda---final.pdf?rev=d3f872755d7d4d80b6608c3ebb09f353) separately placed 29-31 Eldridge Street under “Threatened Properties.”

The library project gives the town a substantial public investment at stake. [Connecticut Public reporting republished by CT Mirror](https://ctmirror.org/2026/07/09/manchester-net-zero-library/) described the new facility as a 75,000-square-foot, all-electric, net-zero-energy public library with solar arrays, battery storage and geothermal heating and cooling. The project was designed to address shortcomings at the older Mary Cheney Library, including limited study, meeting and parking space. That context explains why Manchester is pressing for additional parking, but it also means the preservation fight is testing whether a new civic facility can expand without sacrificing a historic resource next door.

The next decision belongs to the attorney general’s office, which will review materials from the council before deciding whether to begin a legal process, according to CT Insider. The council’s vote is not itself a final court order, and the available public reports do not establish whether demolition work has been scheduled or whether the town will revise its plan. For now, the unresolved questions are whether the home can be preserved or adaptively reused, whether fewer parking spaces can meet the library’s needs, and whether the state will seek a formal intervention before Manchester moves forward.
